title: Adab of the market
hook: a hand pushed into a heap of grain comes out wet

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of the road, and your line: the road's rights. The street owes, and is owed.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is walking through the market, past a seller's heap of grain. He pushes his hand into it, deep, and his fingers come out wet. It's in Sahih Muslim. He asks the seller what this is. Rain got to it, the seller says. And the Prophet answers, in paraphrase: then why didn't you put the wet part on top, so people could see it? Then one short sentence about anyone who cheats, and it's the hardest line in today's lesson.
screen: `A HAND IN THE GRAIN.` → `WET UNDERNEATH.` → `WHY NOT PUT IT ON TOP?`

segments.voice: The sentence is: whoever cheats is not of me. Notice what the seller had done. He hadn't soaked the grain himself; rain did that. His fault was letting the dry grain hide the wet. In this adab, honesty has to be visible. The Qur'an says the same in the language of scales. Al-Mutaffifin, the defrauders, opens like this, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the defrauders: Those who when they take the measure from mankind demand it full, But if they measure unto them or weigh for them, they cause them loss." Full measure when buying, short measure when selling: the verse catches the double standard. Then hoarding. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says, in paraphrase, that no one hoards except a sinner: buying up what people need and holding it back until they're desperate. The market is meant to feed people, not corner them. And the line this day is named for. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: may Allah have mercy on a man who is easygoing when he sells, easygoing when he buys, and easygoing when he asks for what he's owed. The last, collecting a debt, is easy to skip. Another hadith in Bukhari: if buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed; if they hide things and lie, the blessing is wiped away. Honesty you can see, no profiting from need, and ease on both sides of the counter.
screen: `WHOEVER CHEATS IS NOT OF ME.` · `WOE UNTO THE DEFRAUDERS.` · `NO HOARDING.` · `EASY WHEN BUYING, SELLING, ASKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one exchange coming up, a purchase, a bill, a refund, something you're selling, someone who owes you, and notice where you'd usually press hard, or grumble, or let the wet grain stay hidden. Now see it done the hadith's way: a fair price said plainly, any flaw said out loud, and a little more patience than you'd planned for whoever owes you. If you pray, you can ask for barakah, blessing, in your dealings.
Adab of the market. The manners of buying and selling: honest scales, nothing hidden, no hoarding, and ease when you sell, buy, and ask for what you're owed. Today's word.
Your line: easy in dealing. Honesty you can see. That's one thousand three hundred days.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to trade by full measure, disclose a product's faults, avoid hoarding, and be easygoing when buying, selling and collecting debts, citing al-Mutaffifin and the hadith of the heap of grain.

options: Yes. Put the wet grain on top: a hadith says whoever cheats is not of me.
No. If they don't ask, it's the buyer's job to look closely before paying.
Only if the flaw is your fault. Damage from rain or bad luck needn't be said.
